4d74cb48eb9b04e1: PETALING JAYA: Umno perlu membuktikan kesungguhannya dalam soal akauntabiliti dengan meminta bekas menteri pertahanan daripada parti itu tampil menjelaskan keputusan serta pemantauan mereka terhadap projek kapal tempur pesisir (LCS), kata seorang penganalisis.

Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri daripada Global Asia Consulting berkata parti itu juga wajar menyokong penilaian bebas terhadap keputusan kementerian, perubahan kontrak dan langkah pembetulan yang diambil, selain meneliti tanggungjawab kontraktor.
“Akauntabiliti bukan bermaksud menganggap semua pihak bersalah. Ia bermaksud menuntut penjelasan,” katanya.
Beliau berkata mengenakan penalti kontrak terhadap pembina kapal semata-mata tidak akan menjawab persoalan mengenai keputusan yang dibuat dalam Kementerian Pertahanan.
“Jika kontraktor bertanggungjawab terhadap kelewatan, kenakan penalti yang sewajarnya mengikut kontrak.
“Tetapi jika keputusan kementerian turut menyumbang kepada kelewatan itu, siapa pula yang akan mempertanggungjawabkan pihak yang membuat keputusan?” soalnya.
Sejak 2009, portfolio pertahanan pernah diterajui lima pemimpin Umno, iaitu Zahid Hamidi, Hishammuddin Hussein, Ismail Sabri Yaakob, Mohamad Hasan dan menteri pertahanan ketika ini, Khaled Nordin.
“Tidak semua menteri membuat keputusan yang sama dan tanggungjawab perlu dinilai berdasarkan tempoh masing-masing memegang jawatan,” kata Zaharuddin.
Menurutnya, rekod Umno dalam kerajaan turut membawa tanggungjawab untuk menjelaskan kelemahan dalam pemantauan serta tindakan yang diambil menteri parti itu apabila masalah mula timbul.
Projek itu pada asalnya membabitkan pembinaan enam kapal dengan kos RM9.128 bilion, tetapi kemudian disemak kepada lima kapal dengan kos RM11.227 bilion.
Kapal pertama yang sepatutnya diserahkan pada 2019 kini disasarkan untuk penyerahan fizikal pada April 2027.

Pada 26 Okt, Khaled mengakui ada kelewatan dalam memuktamadkan beberapa kontrak serta perubahan yang diminta Kementerian Pertahanan, namun berkata pembina kapal itu juga ketinggalan daripada jadual pembinaan.
Beliau berkata notis tuntutan ganti rugi sudah dikeluarkan kepada Lumut Naval Shipyard (Lunas), yang akan diberi peluang menjelaskan punca kelewatan.
Ganti rugi akan dikenakan jika penjelasan syarikat itu didapati tidak memuaskan.
Dalam kenyataannya pada 19 Okt, Lunas merujuk kepada beberapa kontrak sokongan yang dikendalikan secara langsung Kementerian Pertahanan serta sekatan eksport peluru berpandu oleh Norway.
Syarikat itu berkata tanggungjawab terhadap kelewatan perlu ditentukan melalui proses yang ditetapkan dalam kontrak.
Penganalisis pertahanan Zaki Salleh pula menggesa Umno mengakui kelemahan pemantauan pada masa lalu dan mendapatkan penjelasan daripada bekas menteri pertahanan mengenai asas keputusan yang dibuat.
Katanya, parti itu boleh menunjukkan akauntabiliti melalui beberapa langkah praktikal.
“Antaranya memberikan penjelasan secara terbuka, menyokong penelitian bebas dan melaksanakan pembaharuan dasar,” katanya.
Zaki turut menggesa Umno menyokong siasatan Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM) dan penelitian Jawatankuasa Kira-kira Wang Negara (PAC), tanpa menolaknya sebagai serangan politik.

Bagaimanapun, katanya, penilaian yang adil juga perlu mengambil kira kelemahan tadbir urus korporat dan pengurusan kontrak, selain perkembangan luar yang berada di luar kawalan parti politik tempatan.
Penganalisis keselamatan Mizan Aslam daripada Global Peace Institute of London turut berkata Umno perlu bertanggungjawab menjelaskan bagaimana projek LCS boleh berdepan masalah.
“Saya mahu tahu mengapa perkara ini berlaku dan ke mana wang itu dibelanjakan,” katanya.
Mizan berkata, menyiapkan kapal berkenaan sahaja tidak akan menjawab persoalan mengenai masa, wang dan sumber yang telah hilang, serta siapa yang sepatutnya dipertanggungjawabkan.
Beliau mengingatkan supaya Umno tidak dipersalahkan secara menyeluruh, namun berkata parti itu boleh berbuat lebih banyak untuk memastikan pihak yang bertanggungjawab dikenakan tindakan.
Katanya, langkah sedemikian juga boleh membantu Umno membina semula kepercayaan rakyat.
aea771317688be96: PETALING JAYA: Umno should show it is serious about accountability by asking former defence ministers from the party to publicly explain their decisions and oversight of the littoral combat ship (LCS) project, a political analyst says.

Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri of Global Asia Consulting said the party should also support an independent assessment of ministerial decisions, contract changes and corrective actions alongside scrutiny of the contractor’s obligations.
“Accountability does not mean declaring everyone guilty. It means demanding answers,” he said.
He argued that pursuing contractual penalties against the shipbuilder would not, by itself, answer questions about decisions made within the defence ministry.
“If the contractor is responsible for delays, impose the appropriate contractual penalties.
“But if ministry decisions contributed to those delays, who holds the decision-makers accountable,” he asked.
Between 2009 and now, Umno’s Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, Hishammuddin Hussein, Ismail Sabri Yaakob, Mohamad Hasan and current defence minister Khaled Nordin have all held the defence portfolio.
“Not every minister made the same decisions, and responsibility must be assessed according to their respective tenures,” Zaharuddin said.
He said Umno’s record in government carried an obligation to explain shortcomings in supervision and what its ministers did when problems emerged.
The project originally involved six ships costing RM9.128 billion, but was subsequently revised to five at RM11.227 billion.
The first ship, originally due in 2019, is now targeted for physical handover in April 2027.
On Oct 26, Khaled acknowledged delays in finalising certain contracts and changes requested by the defence ministry, but said the shipbuilder had also fallen behind schedule in its construction work.

He said a notice of demand for damages had been issued to Lumut Naval Shipyard (Lunas), which would be given an opportunity to explain the delays, and that damages would be imposed if its explanation was found to be unsatisfactory.

In its Oct 19 statement, Lunas pointed to supporting contracts handled directly by the defence ministry and Norwegian missile export restrictions, saying responsibility for the delays should be assessed through the contractual process.
Defence analyst Zaki Salleh urged Umno to acknowledge past oversight weaknesses and seek explanations from former defence ministers about the basis of their decisions.
He said the party could demonstrate accountability through several practical measures.
“These include providing open explanations, supporting independent scrutiny, and implementing policy reforms,” he said.
Zaki called on Umno to support Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission investigations and Public Accounts Committee scrutiny without dismissing them as political attacks.

However, he stressed that a fair assessment must also consider weaknesses in corporate governance and contract management, as well as external developments beyond the control of domestic political parties.
Security analyst Mizan Aslam of Global Peace Institute of London, also said Umno should assume responsibility for explaining how the LCS project went wrong.
“I want to know why this thing happened and where the money has gone,” he said.
Mizan argued that completing the vessels would leave unanswered questions about the time, money and resources lost, and who should be held accountable.
He cautioned against blaming Umno indiscriminately, but said the party could do more to ensure those responsible are held accountable.
Taking such steps could help Umno rebuild public trust, he added.
df69c05e3337822c: PETALING JAYA: You may think you know your dog pretty well. But while that familiar face might be easy to read when dinner is late or a walk is overdue, scientists are still discovering just how dogs perceive the humans and objects around them.

Recent studies suggest our canine companions may be capable of connecting a person's voice with their age, associating particular sounds with visual shapes, and even developing a taste for an unusual new source of protein.
Here are three intriguing recent discoveries about man's best friend.
1. Dogs may connect a child's voice with a child's face
Can your dog tell that a child's voice belongs to a younger person before seeing who is speaking?

Researchers recently tested 69 pet dogs by playing recordings of either an adult woman or a young girl before showing them a photograph of an adult or child. Sometimes the voice and face belonged to the same age group; sometimes they did not.
The dogs showed a tendency to look longer when voices and faces matched. Intriguingly, this pattern appeared stronger among dogs that had lived with young children.

Scientists, however, describe the evidence as tentative: the overall effect was weak, and the dogs behaved differently from what researchers originally predicted. As such, the finding cannot yet be taken as proof that dogs neatly sort humans into "child" and "adult" categories.

Still, dogs are already known to combine information from different senses when interpreting people, including clues involving emotion and identity. This latest research raises the possibility that everyday experience with children might also teach them something about what younger humans look and sound like.
2. ‘Bouba’ may look round - even to a dog
Try saying the words "bouba" and "kiki". If asked to match them with two imaginary shapes, many people instinctively pair "bouba" with something round and "kiki" with something sharp and spiky.
This concept - which has been around since the 20th century - is known as the "bouba-kiki effect”. Scientists once wondered whether it might be closely tied to human language.

But dogs, apparently, may be in on it, too: researchers at the University of Parma in Italy tested 70 adult dogs, showing them rounded and spiky shapes while repeatedly playing the sounds "bouba" or "kiki".

The dogs spent more time looking at the rounded shape when they heard "bouba", and at the spiky one when they heard "kiki". A second group was tested while their owners wore headphones, helping researchers rule out the possibility that humans were unintentionally influencing their pets.
The findings suggest the connection between certain sounds and shapes may not be uniquely human - or even dependent on language.
Exactly why the brain makes these connections remains an open question. But next time you tell your dog something is "kiki", don't be entirely surprised if he expects it to have pointy bits.
3. Dogs may enjoy kibble made with microbial protein
The future of dog food may contain an ingredient that sounds considerably less appetising to humans: protein produced by microorganisms.
A recent study tested dry food containing 10% microbial protein on 30 dogs, alongside a comparable diet using conventional protein sources.

Given a choice between the two over four meals, the dogs showed a significant preference for the microbial-protein food. They consumed more of it overall and were also somewhat more likely to approach and begin eating it first.
Cats were included in the research, too, and showed a similar preference.
Microbial protein is being explored as an alternative ingredient partly because it can be produced in controlled systems without relying as heavily on conventional animal agriculture.

But the researchers stressed that their experiment looked only at short-term food preference. It does not demonstrate that such diets are better for pets, nor does it establish their long-term health effects.
The study was also conducted by researchers affiliated with MicroHarvest, the company that produced the microbial protein, making independent follow-up particularly important.

Taken together, the studies don't suddenly reveal what's going on inside every dog's head or food bowl. But they do suggest that behind those familiar puppy-dog eyes lies a sensory world scientists are only beginning to understand.

6773e349a37f1057: SEOUL: North Korea test-fired strategic cruise missiles, state media reported Tuesday, in the latest display of its weapons capabilities as tensions persist on the Korean peninsula.

The Monday launch came a day after North Korea tested cluster bomb warheads, as tensions with Seoul have risen after a landmine blast along their heavily fortified border wounded three South Korean soldiers.

"The middle-sized dispersal warhead tipped on the cruise missile is capable of turning into ashes a target area of 5 to 6 hectares with its highest-density power," the official Korean Central News Agency reported Tuesday.

The test "perfected the capability to deliver a vertical strike against the target by improving the terminal manoeuvrability of the cruise missile", KCNA said, "taking into consideration the natural and geographical characteristics of the targeted area."
A North Korean official was quoted as saying the test was conducted "because our armed forces should defend the security of the country and deter all sorts of threats."

"Various combat functions of such a strongest weapon system will help defend the DPRK from potential threats from outside and renew the military capabilities of the state," the general director of the Missile Administration said, using the acronym for North Korea's official name.
The nuclear-armed North recently trialled a range of weaponry including attack drones, a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
South Korea's military did not announce the cruise missile launch, as it had also not done with Sunday's test.
Unlike ballistic missile launches, North Korean cruise missile tests are not prohibited by UN Security Council sanctions.

Asked Monday about Sunday's reported test, Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young said South Korea and the United States were "closely coordinating and conducting a highly detailed analysis of its characteristics and specifications".
"Our military does not announce all projectiles launched by North Korea," said Jang.

"Whether to make an announcement is determined through a comprehensive military assessment, taking into account the protection of surveillance and reconnaissance assets and capabilities, operational security and other factors," he added.

f06c221a109ea56f: KUALA LUMPUR: Binance's bid to regain a foothold in Malaysia could face tougher regulatory scrutiny following a US$6.3 billion (RM25.6 billion) security breach that has renewed concerns over the cryptocurrency exchange's ability to protect customer assets.

Industry players contacted by Business Times said the incident raises questions about Binance's cybersecurity safeguards, operational resilience and capacity to manage risks, potentially complicating its efforts to secure regulatory approval in Malaysia.

The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange confirmed it had been engaging the Securities Commission (SC) and Bank Negara Malaysia over the past 10 months to explore a licensed route to offer its products and services locally.
On Oct 31, a Binance spokesperson reportedly said discussions centred on the viability and structure of a licensed business model, but declined to disclose the specific licence being sought.

Halogen Capital founder and chief executive officer Hann Liew said the timing was challenging for Binance's regional team as it pursued registration as a registered market operator for digital asset exchanges.

He said the scale of the security breach would shift regulators' attention towards operational resilience and systemic risks, with the SC and Bank Negara likely to scrutinise the incident's root cause, remediation measures and safeguards for local customer assets.

"We expect both the SC and Bank Negara to conduct deep-dive inquiries into the incident's root cause, scrutinise post-mortem remediation and process enhancements, and demand absolute certainty that local Malaysian client assets and infrastructure can be completely ringfenced from offshore operational vulnerabilities," he added.

Liew said regulators will place significant weight on an exchange's cybersecurity and compliance track record, adding that digital asset custody and security remained among the industry's most important considerations.
"In fact, in our experience, digital asset custody and security is the highest-weighted item for our industry. Anything other than global best practices will no longer be sufficient," he added.

Beyond cybersecurity, Liew said regulators will also examine Binance's integrity, internal process controls and financial resilience, particularly given indications that human vulnerabilities and social engineering played a role in the breach.
He said independent third-party post-mortems and audits, evidence of corrective measures and the local segregation of customer assets would be important considerations before approval was granted.

KDX chief executive officer Chan Wei Chi said the security breach was only one aspect of the SC's broader assessment, with Binance still needing to demonstrate its ability to meet other regulatory requirements.
These include having sufficient local manpower, governance structures and adequate capital to support its Malaysian operations.
Chan said regulators should place significant emphasis on the exchange's global security track record, given that operators were responsible for safeguarding customers' assets.
He said Malaysian digital asset exchanges had so far avoided major security breaches by adopting conservative approaches to their operations and asset protection.
"The SC should assess Binance's operational DNA and determine whether it is inherently a risk-taking or conservative organisation.
"If it wants to secure a licence here, it must demonstrate that it can comply with local regulations while adopting a more conservative approach to its operations," he added.

Chan said Binance's global standing should not automatically translate into regulatory approval, noting that its operating practices would need to be assessed against the standards expected of local exchanges.
Chan further commented that Binance's security breach and regulatory history could weigh on its ability to build trust among Malaysian investors.
The company's growth had taken place largely outside the scrutiny of regulators, he added.

"Binance has become the largest player, but it got to where it is today without having to answer to regulators. It has been able to operate on its own terms, placing commercial growth above many other factors," he said.
Chan said the exchange will need to demonstrate its willingness to comply with local requirements and meet the standards established by existing Malaysian operators.
"The biggest question is whether Binance is prepared to abide by and respect Malaysia's regulatory requirements," he said.

The latest incident could add another layer to Binance's regulatory challenges in Malaysia, where the SC ordered the exchange to cease operating in July 2021 after finding that it had illegally operated a digital asset exchange without registration.
Although Binance was removed from the SC's Investor Alert List in 2024, it was added back on Oct 8 this year.
The security breach, which occurred on Oct 29, involved about US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency assets and was reportedly the largest known crypto heist.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group.
In response, Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while investigating the breach and working with law enforcement agencies and industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen assets.
About US$3 billion was reportedly frozen on-chain, while Binance pledged to cover affected customers' losses using its corporate treasury and Secure Asset Fund for Users.
The exchange said it had replenished about 95 per cent of the affected assets and began restoring withdrawals in phases.

Liew said Binance had taken steps to restore confidence by making investors whole using its corporate balance sheet, but its longer-term credibility would depend on improvements to its security protocols and internal processes.
"What remains to be seen is their enhancements to their process or security protocols to ensure a hack of this size and nature becomes impossible going forward," he said.
Separately, Binance has also faced questions over the use of its peer-to-peer (P2P) platform to facilitate ringgit transactions through advertisements listed under other currency denominations.

Business Times has reached out to the SC and Bank Negara for further clarification on Binance's licensing discussions and whether the recent security breach could affect its proposed return to Malaysia.

7f34fcc145681899: SINGAPORE: Grab Holdings raised its full-year revenue and profit forecasts after quarterly earnings beat estimates, signalling confidence that rising ride-hailing and food-delivery demand across Southeast Asia will offset regulatory hurdles.

Sales will rise to US$4.15 billion to US$4.2 billion this year, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation will be as much as US$800 million, the company said Tuesday. In August, it had forecast sales of as much as US$4.15 billion and earnings on that basis of up to US$740 million.
The stock rose about 2% in after-hours trading.

Grab added about 3 million monthly users in the quarter through September for a total of 57 million, suggesting it’s succeeding in fending off intense competition from the likes of Indonesia’s GoTo Group. Demand for ride hailing and food delivery is rising in Southeast Asia as more people go online.

Meanwhile, higher fuel prices are raising ride and delivery costs across the region of about 700 million people. Platform companies are offering incentives to drivers and customers to soften the blow, but that risks squeezing already thin margins.

Regulators are also piling on pressure. Indonesia, one of Grab’s biggest markets, has already cut the maximum commission companies can charge on scooter rides, and is considering further rules in areas like food delivery by the end of the year.
Competition remains intense, with rivals such as GoTo and new entrants like Green & Smart Mobility JSC vying against Grab in populous markets like Indonesia and Vietnam.

Uber Technologies, one of Grab’s backers, could also be a looming threat - its planned acquisition of Delivery Hero SE opens up a path for Uber Eats to re-enter Southeast Asia. Alphabet’s Waymo also plans to launch robotaxis in Singapore in 2028.
Shares of Grab have dropped more than 40% since the start of the year, cutting its market value to about US$11 billion.

The company, meanwhile, is striking deals to spur growth beyond its core business. In September, it agreed to acquire a majority stake in buy-now-pay-later platform Atome Financial for US$1.49 billion, after buying US-based Stash Financial for an enterprise value of US$425 million.
But not every deal has gone to plan. Last month, Taiwan’s Fair Trade Commission blocked Grab’s roughly US$600 million purchase of Foodpanda’s local delivery operations on antitrust concerns.

In the latest quarter, adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose 74% to US$237 million, the Singapore-based company said. Analysts projected US$194.2 million on average, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Revenue grew 27% to US$1.1 billion, roughly in line with estimates.

To add users, Grab has expanded its product offering to include more affordable and premium options. It’s also expanding into games and microdramas, partnering with other platforms to keep users on its app for longer.
25063ef0ee70a380: PETALING JAYA: Seorang kanak-kanak yang dilahirkan di Malaysia tetapi ibu bapa kandungnya tidak dapat dikenal pasti berhak mendapat kewarganegaraan Malaysia secara kuat kuasa undang-undang, menurut keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi Ipoh.
Hakim Moses Susayan berkata kerajaan gagal membuktikan bahawa kanak-kanak itu merupakan warga negara lain atau ibu kandungnya bukan pemastautin tetap di Malaysia.
Beliau berkata kanak-kanak itu tidak sepatutnya menanggung akibat daripada maklumat palsu yang diberikan oleh orang dewasa yang bertanggungjawab mendaftarkan kelahirannya.
“Kanak-kanak itu tidak mempunyai suara dalam proses pendaftaran asal dan tidak melakukan sebarang penipuan,” katanya dalam alasan penghakiman setebal 25 muka surat.

Kes itu membabitkan permohonan sepasang suami isteri yang mengambil kanak-kanak berkenaan sebagai anak angkat, bagi pihak mereka sendiri serta sebagai wakil litigasi kanak-kanak itu, selepas Jabatan Pendaftaran Negara (JPN) menggugurkan nama mereka sebagai ibu bapa daripada rekod kelahiran asal.

Pasangan itu pada mulanya mendaftarkan kanak-kanak berkenaan sebagai anak kandung mereka sebelum JPN mendapati mereka bukan ibu bapa kandungnya. Sijil kelahiran yang dikeluarkan kemudian menyatakan maklumat ibu bapanya tidak tersedia.
Pemohon kedua (ibu angkat) didakwa berhubung maklumat palsu yang diberikan ketika proses pendaftaran dan dikenakan hukuman sewajarnya. Pasangan itu kemudiannya memperoleh perintah pengangkatan.
Bagaimanapun, JPN menyenaraikan kanak-kanak itu sebagai bukan warganegara.

Susayan memutuskan bahawa kanak-kanak itu layak mendapat kewarganegaraan di bawah Seksyen 1(a) Bahagian II, dibaca bersama Seksyen 19B Bahagian III Jadual Kedua Perlembagaan Persekutuan, yang memperuntukkan anggapan kewarganegaraan bagi bayi baru lahir yang ditemukan terbiar.
Beliau berkata peruntukan itu perlu ditafsirkan secara luas bagi melindungi bayi yang ditinggalkan dan ibu bapa kandungnya tidak dapat dikesan.
“Kanak-kanak itu tidak sepatutnya menanggung akibat kesalahan orang dewasa serta siasatan yang tidak dapat memberikan kesimpulan,” katanya.

Hakim itu turut mendapati kanak-kanak berkenaan layak mendapat kewarganegaraan di bawah Seksyen 1(e), memandangkan tiada bukti menunjukkan kanak-kanak itu merupakan warga negara lain atau memperoleh kewarganegaraan asing dalam tempoh setahun selepas kelahirannya.
Beliau menolak hujah kerajaan bahawa pasangan itu bertanggungjawab membuktikan kanak-kanak berkenaan bukan warga negara mana-mana negara lain.
Mahkamah mengarahkan JPN dan kerajaan membetulkan rekod kelahiran kanak-kanak itu serta mengeluarkan sijil kelahiran dan MyKad yang mengiktirafnya sebagai warganegara Malaysia dalam tempoh 30 hari.
Agalya Munusamy dan Kritika Padmanapan mewakili ibu bapa angkat itu, manakala Peguam Kanan Persekutuan Norazlinawati Arshad mewakili kerajaan.
3753159b1c965b29: KUALA LUMPUR: I was watching Ms Rachel with my children recently when her song “I Could Be Your Friend” caught my attention.

Its cheerful melody and uplifting lyrics sounded like something Jason Mraz might sing. I even wondered whether the American singer-songwriter had ever worked with the popular children’s YouTube presenter.
Then I thought about “Sesame Street”, where Canadian singer Feist famously turned her hit “1234” into a children’s counting song. Surely Mraz would be perfect for something similar?

A little digging revealed he had beaten me to it. Back in 2009, Mraz had joined Elmo and friends to sing “Outdoors”, a children’s version of his massive hit “I’m Yours”. So much for my brilliant idea.
But it made sense: few musicians have built a career around spreading happiness quite like Mraz, whose songs celebrate love, friendship and finding joy in the little things.
And that was precisely what he brought to the National Hockey Stadium in Bukit Jalil on Saturday night, where some 8,000 fans gathered for his first Malaysian concert in seven years.

I brought my nine-year-old daughter, who was attending her first concert, wondering whether Mraz would be a suitable introduction to live music for someone her age. But those concerns quickly disappeared.

There was already something to marvel at before Mraz even appeared. A spectacular drone show lit up the sky for around 20 minutes, with hundreds of synchronised lights forming dazzling shapes overhead.
The weather, however, was less cooperative. Intermittent showers interrupted the first 30 to 45 minutes, but the rain soon passed.
Mraz took to the stage at 8.28pm, opening with “You and I Both”, followed by “Long Drive” and “Living in the Moment”. His voice was as smooth and reassuring as ever.
And here came another pleasant surprise. I'd arrived with my EarPods on, bracing myself for the pounding sound that usually leaves me with a headache. Perhaps it comes with being in your 40s.

Halfway through, I realised I did not need them. The volume felt just right, the vocals were clear and the instruments beautifully balanced. I removed my EarPods and enjoyed the rest of the concert headache-free.

Musically, there was much to enjoy. “Make It Mine”, from his 2008 album “We Sing. We Dance. We Steal Things.”, was one of the night’s highlights. Its infectious rhythm reminded me why I became such a fan.

“A Beautiful Mess”, another personal favourite, was equally satisfying, while a medley featuring “Look for the Good”, “Life Is Wonderful”, “Bella Luna” and “Lucky” showed how comfortably Mraz could move between different stages of his career.

His musicians were excellent, too. Molly Miller impressed on electric guitar, Chaska Potter added warmth and depth on vocals, particularly during “Lucky”, while drummer and percussionist Mona Tavakoli was a joy to watch.

One of the evening’s most touching moments came when Mraz spoke about his childhood friend Charlie Mingroni, whose battle with cancer inspired “The Remedy (I Won’t Worry)”. Mraz told of how Mingroni had faced his illness with courage and a determination not to spend his life worrying.
Happily, his friend is still alive. It gave new meaning to the song, which received a soulful treatment that night.
Behind its upbeat melody was a reminder that Mraz’s music is not simply about being happy, but about finding hope when life becomes difficult.

There was humour, too. Introducing “I Feel Like Dancing”, Mraz recalled writing it around 11 years ago, when dancing seemed like a wonderful idea. These days, he joked, he would rather sit or, better still, lie down.

For all the positive energy coming from the stage, the audience in my section was surprisingly reserved. A handful of enthusiastic fans stood up and danced, while many others remained seated, offering polite applause between songs.

Perhaps it was the premium seating, where the atmosphere occasionally felt more like a corporate dinner than a concert. Then again, this was an all-seated event, and Mraz’s music is hardly the sort that demands everyone jump to their feet.
A few favourites left behind

My bigger disappointment, however, was the setlist. “We Sing. We Dance. We Steal Things.” holds a special place in my music collection. I'd bought the double-CD edition years ago and loved practically every track.

Mraz certainly gave the album its due, performing several songs from it. But I had hoped for more of his playful side, particularly “Butterfly”. I would also have loved to hear “Curbside Prophet”, one of my favourites from his earlier days.

I particularly missed the chemistry of Mraz’s early performances with percussionist Toca Rivera, whom he once jokingly introduced as the "sixth member of the Jackson Five" during a live rendition of “Curbside Prophet”.

Of course, that is the limitation with attending a concert by an artiste whose music has been part of your life for so long. Everyone arrives with a different playlist in their head, and no performer can satisfy them all.

By the time Mraz closed the evening with “I’m Yours”, the audience had found its collective voice. It was the singalong everyone had been waiting for, and a fitting end to a thoroughly enjoyable performance.

Was it everything I had hoped for? Not completely. But between the wonderful musicians, heartfelt stories, familiar melodies and remarkably comfortable sound, Mraz delivered what he does best: music that makes the world feel a little kinder.

And perhaps that's what made it such a fitting first concert for my daughter. I had gone in wondering whether she was ready for Jason Mraz. By the end, I realised his music was perfectly suited to the occasion.
As for her father, he left the stadium happy, headache-free, but still wishing Mraz had played “Butterfly”.
FMT Lifestyle attended the concert with complimentary tickets provided by Zeus Event Sdn Bhd.
a38e848240d6b31c: PETALING JAYA: A child born in Malaysia whose biological parents remain unidentified is entitled to Malaysian citizenship by operation of law, the High Court in Ipoh has ruled.
Justice Moses Susayan said the government had failed to establish that the child was a citizen of another country or that his biological mother was not permanently resident in Malaysia.
He said the child should not be made to suffer because of false information supplied by the adults responsible for his original registration.
“The child had no voice in the original registration and committed no fraud,” he said in his 25-page grounds of judgment.

The case concerned an application by an adoptive couple, acting on their own behalf and as litigation representatives of the child, after the national registration department (JPN) removed their names as parents from the original birth record.

The couple had initially registered the child as their own before the JPN discovered they were not its biological parents. A subsequent birth certificate recorded the parental particulars as unavailable.
The second applicant (the adopted mother) was prosecuted over the false information supplied during the registration process and punished accordingly. The couple later obtained an adoption order.
However, the child was listed by JPN as a non-citizen.

Susayan ruled that the child qualified for citizenship under Section 1(a) of Part II, read with Section 19B of Part III of the Federal Constitution's Second Schedule, which provides a presumption for newborn children found abandoned.
He said the provision must be interpreted broadly to protect abandoned newborns whose biological parents cannot be traced.
“The child should not bear the consequences of both the adults’ wrongdoing and an inconclusive investigation,” he said.
The judge also found that the child qualified under Section 1(e), as there was no evidence to show it was a citizen of another country or had acquired foreign citizenship within one year of birth.
He rejected the government's contention that the onus was on the couple to prove that the child was not a citizen of any other country.
The court ordered JPN and government to rectify the child's birth records and issue a birth certificate and MyKad reflecting its Malaysian citizenship within 30 days.
Agalya Munusamy and Kritika Padmanapan appeared for the adopted parents, while senior federal counsel Norazlinawati Arshad represented the government.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government. Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.

Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.
The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.
This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.

Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.
Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event.

We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications.

Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments.
The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments.

The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate.

Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities.

Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions.
Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice.
The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo.
The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities.

The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them.
We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.

00eafebca583d7b9: SEOUL: North Korea on Tuesday slammed the FBI's allegations that Pyongyang was behind the theft of US$6 billion from cryptocurrency platform Binance, with Kim Jong Un's powerful sister labelling it a "grave political provocation."

Kim Yo Jong, in a statement released Tuesday by the KCNA state news agency, said the FBI's claim was "absurd rhetoric and nothing new," given prior US allegations that North Korea was behind last year's major hack of Bybit.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," Kim said, using the acronym for North Korea's official name.
The FBI said on Saturday that a North Korea-affiliated hacking group called TraderTraitor had been behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a US$1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year, which had been the largest crypto theft until the Binance hack.
"This is a sinister attempt to damage the international image of the DPRK and undermine its dignity and national prestige and another grave violation of the sovereignty of the DPRK," Kim said.
"It is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace," she added.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
After the FBI released its statement on Saturday, US President Donald Trump cast doubt on North Korea's involvement in the hack.
"I'm not concerned. We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea," Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida.
Trump has made repeated overtures to nuclear-armed North Korea since returning to office, and said he was open to meeting with supreme leader Kim Jong Un this year.
Those gestures have been met with silence from Pyongyang.
Kim Yo Jong, in her statement, said the new allegations "confirmed Washington's hostile attitude toward the DPRK once again."
"We have issues to reconsider in diverse aspects as regards the very unpleasant US hostile attitude," she added.--AFP
e3645bbac139f482: PETALING JAYA: Cemburu dipercayai punca lima lelaki bergaduh menggunakan parang di depan sebuah pangsapuri di Taman Cendana, Pasir Gudang, Ahad lalu.
Ketua Polis Seri Alam, Sohaimi Ishak, berkata seorang lelaki tempatan parah yang dikejarkan ke Hospital Pasir Gudang dalam kejadian kira-kira 12.18 tengah malam itu, dilaporkan dalam keadaan stabil.
Menurutnya, seorang lelaki tempatan dalam lingkungan 30 tahun ditahan kira-kira 4.34 pagi 1 Nov lalu susulan video 18 saat yang tular di media sosial.
"Polis turut merampas sebilah parang yang dipercayai digunakan ketika kejadian bagi membantu siasatan," katanya menurut Sinar Harian.
Beliau berkata, hasil semakan mendapati suspek mempunyai lapan rekod kesalahan lampau membabitkan jenayah dan dadah, dengan ujian saringan awal air kencing suspek didapati positif methamphetamine.
Kes disiasat mengikut Seksyen 326 Kanun Keseksaan kerana sengaja menyebabkan kecederaan parah menggunakan senjata atau benda berbahaya serta Seksyen 15(1)(a) Akta Dadah Berbahaya 1952.
Sohaimi berkata, suspek direman tujuh hari sehingga 7 Nov ini dan polis giat mengesan individu lain yang dipercayai terbabit dalam kejadian itu.
Orang ramai yang mempunyai maklumat diminta menghubungi balai polis berhampiran atau Pusat Kawalan Daerah Seri Alam di talian 07-3864222.
f207f138bfe2f5c0: GENEVA: Dozens of global health and environmental organisations called on the World Health Organization on Tuesday to revise decades-old standards for nitrate levels in drinking water, arguing they do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.

In an open letter, 85 organisations, including Greenpeace International and the World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA), called on the United Nations health agency to include nitrate in an upcoming review of its drinking water guidelines.
The toxic effects of nitrates - a residue left behind by intensive farming - are widely recognised as particularly dangerous for children and pregnant women.

But the current WHO guidelines - which set the maximum acceptable nitrate level in drinking water at 50 milligrammes per litre as nitrate or 11.3 milligrammes per litre as nitrate-nitrogen - date back to 1958 and are "outdated", the organisations warned.
That level was set specifically to prevent so-called "blue-baby syndrome" - a deadly blood disorder in which the blood's capacity for carrying oxygen is reduced.

But the limit "has not been updated in response to robust epidemiological evidence linking chronic, low-level nitrate exposure to long-term human health risks", Tuesday's letter said, pointing in particular to "colorectal cancer and adverse birth outcomes".
"Studies now link nitrate in drinking water, at levels well below the current WHO limit, to bowel cancer and premature birth," WONCA chair Pratyush Kumar said in a joint statement.
The letter was sent to coincide with WHO's annual One Health Day, which aims to raise awareness about the interconnected health of humans, animals, plants and shared ecosystems.
Surface water models indicate that hundreds of millions of people globally are exposed to elevated nitrate levels, the letter warned.
"Water should be life-giving, not life-threatening," Amanda Larsson, the global project lead for agriculture at Greenpeace, said in the statement.
"We cannot protect human health without protecting the groundwater and rivers that sustain us," she insisted.

"Governments must take decisive action to curb the growth of intensive livestock farming and actively support producers in transitioning to ecological farming practices - ensuring that clean, safe drinking water isn't a luxury but a guarantee."

The organisations pointed to findings published last year by an expert panel commissioned by the Danish government indicating that the current international standard was insufficient to protect public health.
That expert panel recommended reducing the nitrate limit to 6.0 mg/L - nearly 10 times below the current WHO benchmark - something Denmark committed to earlier this year.
But most national governments base their drinking water standards on WHO guidelines, the organisations said, stressing that updating those guidelines was "vital for global policy reform".
7cda3d78d6fdd916: NEW YORK: Weather conditions are a "major" focus of an investigation into a weekend private plane crash that killed nine people, US transportation investigators said Monday.

At a briefing, Tom Chapman of the National Transportation Safety Board retraced the ill-fated journey of the Learjet 60, which departed Austin, Texas, at 1537 GMT Sunday on a trip to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.
The plane plummeted into a neighbourhood in Palm Beach County in southern Florida, killing everyone on board.
The jet was carrying a pilot, a copilot and seven passengers. Authorities have not released their identities, saying genetic analysis is needed.
US media identified the copilot as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgeiras, who had received her pilot's licence at age 17, before she received a driver's licence.
Filgeiras, who had already amassed 1,300 flight hours, began working for a charter plane company based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida about nine months ago.
Investigators have not determined yet who was flying the plane when it encountered trouble.
In an audio recording posted to air traffic website liveatc.net, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and saying the crew was "managing the ice".
The person said the plane was "picking up precipitation" and needed "to climb" shortly before saying, "Mayday, mayday, we're descending 10,000 feet per minute."
Chapman confirmed these statements had been made to air traffic controllers.

Aircraft maintenance records show there had previously been a cockpit recorder on the plane, but the NTSB doesn't know if it was on the jet at the time of the crash or if the agency will be able to recover it, Chapman said.
NTSB investigator Tim Monville said there was also an injury to a driver in the area near the crash site.
NTSB officials said the aircraft was flown by Aurora Aviation, which was operating as Upper Jets. Officials with the companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment from AFP.
The Bombardier plane went into service in 2004 and was renovated in 2018, according to Jettly.
The owner of the plane is listed as a Delaware company known as LR60271 LLC, according to the website of the US Federal Aviation Administration.
d0e19730fbdf47d6: PARIS: As Paris Saint-Germain head to Spain to face Villarreal on Tuesday, the French club's quest to win a third consecutive Champions League title is under threat as injuries to key players raise doubts about the strength of their squad for another tilt at European glory.
PSG's thrilling 4-2 win two weeks ago against Barcelona was overshadowed by the sight of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia having to be helped off injured in the second half.
The Georgian was probably the best player in last season's Champions League knockout rounds, with seven goals and four assists in eight games up to and including the final against Arsenal.
But the rupture to the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee which the 25-year-old suffered in the win over Barcelona means he is unlikely to return this season.
That is a hammer blow for PSG, who have become Europe's outstanding club side since Kvaratskhelia joined from Napoli in January last year.

Luis Enrique's team began this season's league phase with three wins from three and are well set to reach the knockout stage, but PSG must now be mulling whether to sign a replacement for Kvaratskhelia in the January transfer window.
"Not especially. No injury means we need to sign a new player. None," Luis Enrique said when asked if PSG now needed to go shopping.

"I already said at the start of the season that our team could stay the same, even with two or three injuries. That said, we are always open to the possibility of new players. But not just because we have injuries."
- BARCOLA MISSED? -
PSG had already taken something of a risk by selling Bradley Barcola to Liverpool in August in a blockbuster 145 million-euro (US$162m) transfer.
Goncalo Ramos, Lee Kang-in and Ibrahim Mbaye all made significant attacking contributions in the last two seasons, but were allowed to leave too.
However, Luis Enrique described the business done by the club during the summer as "exceptional", saying: "I am very happy to begin the season with the number of players that we have."
PSG signed Maghnes Akliouche, a French international winger or midfielder, from Monaco and Spain's World Cup final match-winner Ferran Torres from Barcelona, each for a reported 50 million euros.
They also recruited Belgian international winger Mika Godts from Ajax for a reported 55 million euros.
Torres scored seven goals in his first six appearances, but has gone six games without finding the net. Godts got off to a slow start but has just scored in back-to-back games.

But as the new signings settle, there are renewed doubts about Ousmane Dembele's ability to stay fit after he suffered a hamstring injury against Barcelona – a player whose minutes were very carefully managed last season is now out for several weeks.
And it is not just in attack where PSG have injuries, with centre-back and captain Marquinhos and left-back Nuno Mendes sidelined.
In that case, perhaps the answer to all their problems is right-back Achraf Hakimi, scorer of a hat-trick in Friday's 5-1 win at Le Havre in Ligue 1.
"He is more of an attacker," said Luis Enrique, who has overseen more wins than any other coach in PSG's history.
"He plays higher up the pitch and has the ability to make runs and set up goals.
"He is the best right-back in the world. What I like is that he is always at the highest level, always ready. That means a lot."
PSG made it nine straight wins in that game, despite having only two starters from last season's Champions League final in their line-up.
With competition to PSG lacking in France, being able to rest key players in Ligue 1 and still win remains something which could help them when it comes to Europe.
"We are going to need everyone if we are going to win trophies, and with the injuries there will be opportunities," insisted Luis Enrique.
The problem is there are few players anywhere who could adequately replace a talent like Kvaratskhelia.-AFP

1a7942fb3b9f842f: Diplomacy is not always measured by grand agreements, historic handshakes or comprehensive peace settlements.
Sometimes, its effectiveness is demonstrated through small but tangible improvements in human lives.
The recent decision by Myanmar’s military authorities to begin releasing ethnic Rakhine deportees following Malaysian diplomatic pressure is one such development.
According to The Irrawaddy, the releases followed Malaysia’s intervention over the detention of individuals deported from Malaysia to Myanmar.
This is hardly a diplomatic breakthrough. Yet it is not insignificant.
It demonstrates that Putrajaya’s decision to maintain engagement with Nay Pyi Taw, despite international criticism, can produce limited but measurable results.
More baby steps are needed.
First, engagement must never be confused with endorsement.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has faced criticism for engaging Myanmar’s military leadership, particularly Senior General now President Min Aung Hlaing.
Critics argue that such engagement risks legitimising a regime responsible for widespread displacement, military violence and the destruction of democratic institutions.
These concerns are valid.

However, refusing to communicate with the authorities exercising power in Nay Pyi Taw would make it harder for Malaysia to secure detainees’ release, negotiate humanitarian access or protect vulnerable returnees.
Diplomacy requires contact, even with governments whose conduct one fundamentally opposes.
The purpose is not to confer legitimacy but to influence behaviour.
Second, the releases demonstrate the potential value of sustained diplomatic pressure.
Malaysia raised concerns about the treatment of its deportees. Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan sought clarification. Myanmar subsequently began releasing those detained.
Although this sequence does not prove that Malaysian pressure alone led to the releases, it suggests that diplomatic intervention mattered.
Malaysia did not merely accept Myanmar’s treatment of the deportees. It demanded accountability.
This is how engagement should function: dialogue accompanied by expectations, verification and humanitarian safeguards.
Third, piecemeal progress must not conceal Myanmar’s larger humanitarian catastrophe.
Without a doubt, Myanmar remains deeply fractured.
The military authorities do not exercise uncontested control over the entire country.
Ethnic armed organisations and resistance forces remain powerful actors.
Rakhine State is particularly complicated because of the continuing conflict involving the Arakan Army and Myanmar’s military.
Repatriation cannot automatically be considered safe merely because some detainees have been released.
Malaysia must distinguish between voluntary returns and deportations that expose vulnerable people to persecution, detention or forced recruitment.
The principle of non-refoulement must remain central.
Fourth, Malaysia needs stronger mechanisms to monitor returnees.
Diplomatic assurances are meaningful only when independently verified.
Malaysia should work with relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organisations to establish procedures for monitoring the welfare of those returned.
Such arrangements should protect family contact, freedom from arbitrary detention and access to humanitarian assistance.
Without verification, Malaysia risks celebrating releases without knowing whether those individuals subsequently enjoy meaningful security.
Fifth, Asean must translate Malaysia’s incremental progress into collective diplomatic action.
To be sure, the Asean Five-Point Consensus has struggled to end Myanmar’s conflict.
Nevertheless, its fundamental objectives remain relevant: reducing violence, encouraging inclusive dialogue and facilitating humanitarian assistance.
Malaysia’s bilateral engagement should complement these objectives, not replace them.
The Philippines, as Asean Chair in 2026, should consider how such diplomatic openings can strengthen regional cooperation.
Asean needs more than repeated expressions of concern.
It needs Asean’s resolve to translate principles into practical humanitarian outcomes.
Sixth, engagement must extend beyond Myanmar’s military leadership.
Malaysia should maintain communication with the National Unity Government (the Myanmar government-in-exile), ethnic armed organisations, civil society and humanitarian networks.
Myanmar’s fragmentation makes broader engagement indispensable.
A settlement negotiated exclusively with military authorities cannot guarantee acceptance throughout the country.
Malaysia must broaden and deepen its diplomatic channels without abandoning humanitarian principles.
Finally, Anwar’s approach should be judged by outcomes rather than appearances.
Malaysia cannot single-handedly resolve Myanmar’s civil war.
But neither should it abandon opportunities to secure modest improvements in human security.
The release of Rakhine deportees is encouraging, although it does not establish that Myanmar has fundamentally changed.
Further progress requires humanitarian access, independent monitoring, safeguards for returnees and eventually inclusive political dialogue.
Myanmar’s crisis cannot be resolved overnight. Yet diplomatic paralysis is not a strategy.
Malaysia must remain principled without becoming immobilised by the complexity of Myanmar’s conflict.
The journey towards peace may begin with small humanitarian concessions rather than spectacular diplomatic breakthroughs.
More baby steps are needed. But genuine, verifiable and sustainable piecemeal progress is still progress.
For Myanmar’s long-suffering people, even modest improvements in human security matter.

de929831445c05d5: Walaupun seminggu sudah berlalu saya terpanggil menulis mengenai Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan dimeterai antara kerajaan, Ahli Parlimen Bersatu, bekas Ahli Parlimen parti itu yang menyokong PMX dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Sebab? Perikatan Nasional memutuskan tidak akan ikut sama yakni tidak akan menandatangani perjanjian itu yang ramai lebih gemar guna istilah Inggerisnya iaitu CSA untuk Confidence and Supply Agreement.
Keengganan PN memeterai CSA bukanlah sesuatu yang memeranjatkan walaupun pendapat umum ialah CSA peluang perkukuh kestabilan politik negara.

Dan kestabilan politik adalah antara prasyarat penting untuk memastikan dasar kerajaan dapat dilaksanakan dengan berkesan dan manfaatnya dapat dirasai rakyat, dalam sebuah negara yang sedang berdepan pelbagai cabaran ekonomi dan tuntutan pembangunan. At least that’s how Segamat MP R Yuneswaran look at it.

PN jelas tidak bersependapat lalu tidak menerima CSA. Itu hak mereka. Cuma yang menarik bagi saya ialah rakan baik PN (khususnya dalam menghadapi PRN Melaka) iaitu Pengerusi BN Zahid Hamidi menyarankan CSA diperluas kepada lebih banyak parti sama ada daripada kerajaan atau pembangkang.

Kata Zahid apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri. Kata-kata ini buat saya tersenyum lebar. Mengapa? Jawapannya di penghujung artikel ini. Lantas pada hemat saya apa yang dikata Zahid amat menarik atas dua sebab.
Sebab pertama kerana saranan Zahid dibuat semasa PN dan BN semakin mesra. Dan apabila PN tolak CSA bererti mereka tolak juga saranan Zahid.
Sebab kedua ialah apabila Zahid berkata (saya ulang ) “apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri”.

Wakil Ummo jadi perdana menteri yang dimaksudkan kita tahu ialah Ismail Sabri Yaakob. Apa yang berlaku? Tentu ramai masih ingat. Pada September 2021, Ismail memeterai apa yang dipanggil memorandum persefahaman dan kestabilan politik dengan Anwar Ibrahim yang waktu itu ketua pembangkang.
Kata Anwar, memorandum itu menjadi kenyataan kerana sikap positif Ismail yang mengambil pendekatan berunding segera dengan pembangkang sebaik dilantik perdana menteri kesembilan.

Perlu dinyatakan memorandum itu bukan CSA per se. Ini diakui Anwar sendiri waktu itu. Apa pun dalam dokumen MoU antara Pakatan Harapan dengan kerajaan pimpinan Ismail, kerajaan menjanjikan sejumlah reformasi dalam jangka waktu tertentu dan juga berjanji untuk tidak membubarkan Parlimen sebelum 31 Julai 2022.

Sebagai balasan PH pula berjanji tidak akan menggunakan undi mereka menggulingkan Ismail atau menyekat Belanjawan 2022 selagi pembaharuan dijanjikan mengikut jadual dan pembangkang dilibatkan dalam perbincangan Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan. Di samping itu PH berjanji membantu usaha kerajaan memerangi wabak Covid-19 yang melanda waktu itu.

Put simply the MoU was a good thing for the country considering the circumstance then. Namun, Zahid dan Umno menekan Ismail untuk mengadakan pilihan raya umum dengan segera kerana berpendapat Umno sedang berada pada tahap meyakinkan untuk menang. Zahid konon mahu Ismail strike while the iron is still hot.
Tindakan Zahid dan Umno boleh dilihat sebagai tidak memberi ruang kepada Ismail menjayakan MoU beliau dengan PH.

Tekanan demi tekanan dikenakan ke atas Ismail. Menyulitkan Ismail ialah beliau sekadar seorang naib presiden Umno manakala Zahid presiden parti . Akhirnya, Ismail tidak ada pilihan melainkan tunduk akur. Parlimen dibubarkan pada Oktober 2022 dan PRU15 diadakan pada November 2022.
Dan Umno/BN mencatat prestasi paling buruk dalam sejarah mereka. Umno hanya menang 27 kerusi, MCA (2) dan MIC (1). Perkiraan Zahid meleset.

Fast forward CSA yang dimeterai 29 Okt lalu. Pada upacara tandatangan kerajaan diketuai Timbalan Perdana Menteri II Fadillah Yusof. Bukan timbalan perdana menteri I. Kita tahu siapa pemegang jawatan itu.
Mungkinkah ini kerana pendirian lalu Zahid terhadap MoU 2021 dan tindakan susulannya yang boleh dilihat sebagai bertentangan dengan semangat MoU itu?
Maka, kerana itulah saya tersenyum lebar seperti disebut tadi apabila Zahid memuji CSA 2026 dan mahu ia diperluas kepada semua parti.

390498bfb300beb9: KUALA LUMPUR: For identical triplets Muhammad Nuriman, Muhammad Nuramin and Muhammad Nurnaim Irwan, becoming soldiers was not just a passing childhood fantasy.
The 21-year-old siblings first tried to join the armed forces in 2023 after finishing secondary school, but were turned away because they did not meet the minimum height requirement.
That setback was followed by more unsuccessful attempts: seven applications to the Malaysian Army and one to the Royal Malaysian Navy. Still, they kept going.
Their chance finally came this year, after the army revised its minimum height requirement for recruits from 162cm to 157cm. At 158cm, all three brothers were now eligible.
As children, the brothers often saw photographs of their grandfather, Ismail Ujang, 80, who served in the navy for 25 years before retiring as a Warrant Officer I.
“We saw his old photographs in his white uniform, and that was when we became interested in becoming soldiers,” Nuramin told Bernama.
Their grandfather’s stories only deepened that fascination: he would tell them about his years in service, including encounters with pirates in the waters off Lahad Datu while stationed in Labuan.

The brothers carried that ambition into adulthood, even as repeated rejection forced them to find other ways forward. They enrolled at the Kuala Lumpur Industrial Training Institute and earned Malaysian Skills Certificate Level 3 qualifications, while continuing to prepare themselves physically and mentally.

They also joined the Territorial Army Regiment and took part in national service training last year. While these experiences did not guarantee them a place in the regular army, they kept the dream alive.
Early this year, all three succeeded in the selection process and began six months of basic military training in Port Dickson. They were among 1,485 recruits who completed the programme on Oct 17.
Nurnaim said one of the hardest parts was the final field exercise, which tested combat skills, teamwork and mental endurance under pressure.
Yet even during the most demanding weeks, there were lighter moments - fellow recruits and instructors frequently struggled to tell the brothers apart.

Their mother, Yusnizah Yusof, 52, said she and her husband had always supported the boys, driving them to selection exercises in Seremban, Kuala Lumpur and Pahang despite the repeated disappointments.
“We spent a lot of time taking them to the various camps where selection exercises were held so they could pursue their dreams,” she said.
Together at last - and now apart
After years of trying to enter the army together, the triplets now face something new: separation. Nuriman has been posted to Ipoh, Nuramin to Kuching and Nurnaim to Johor Bahru.
For three brothers who trained, applied and persevered alongside one another, that marks a major change.
“There is some sadness, of course, but being apart will not stop the three of us from moving forward,” Nurnaim said.

Their grandfather’s old photographs may have sparked the idea years ago, but the rest was theirs: eight disappointments, months of training, and the determination to earn the uniforms they had wanted since childhood.

f8edbaaa89160776: It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light.

In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science.

The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.

4f9deb0e6fcfcd05: WASHINGTON: Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday reported a more than 1,100% surge in quarterly revenue and nearly US$900 billion in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later this month.
The San Francisco-based company was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela, now its president, with AI safety as its focus.
The listing comes amid growing nervousness among investors about the huge sums being poured into AI.

Revenue reached US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier, though sales growth slowed from previous quarters amid fierce competition from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and cheaper models, many of them from China.

The company, whose stock market debut is seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last, said in an amended filing that its net loss reached US$23.3 billion in the July-September period.
The loss stemmed mostly from non-cash accounting charges linked to the company’s rising valuation, the filing showed.
Anthropic also posted an operating loss of US$567 million in the third quarter as it paid more for short-term computing capacity.
The filing said the company has committed to spend about US$895 billion, mostly on computing power, with US$70 billion of that due before September 2027.

The IPO will be a major test of the market's faith in the AI boom, with the pool of potential investors set to widen as retail traders get their first chance to buy shares directly in a standalone AI giant.
According to several media outlets, the five-year-old company plans to raise around $100 billion in its initial public offering, at a valuation of between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion.
That would surpass the record set in June by SpaceX, which raised US$86 billion.
Last week, concerns about AI spending triggered a sharp sell-off in big tech stocks after the latest earnings showed massive investment without clear signs of a return.

Anthropic's roughly 400-page filing devotes more than 90 pages to risks, including those facing an industry that has seen a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.
Anthropic's focus on safety is built into its corporate structure. It is a public benefit corporation, legally required to weigh its mission of developing AI safely alongside shareholder returns.
The co-founders, meanwhile, will hold 50.1% of shareholder voting power through a single special share, leaving investors who buy on the market little say over the company's direction.
The IPO comes as more major companies involved in the AI spending bonanza turn to the markets to finance their ambitions.

Meta and Google parent Alphabet have launched their own fundraising plans on the public markets, and Oracle said Monday it was going ahead with a US$20 billion plan despite doubts about its financial exposure.

9730943e7757b789: SAN FRANCISCO: Snap has settled what would have been another landmark trial over the alleged harms of social media, lawyers for the plaintiffs said Monday, just days after Meta reached its own settlement and two days before opening statements were due to begin in a Los Angeles courtroom.
The case was to be the latest in a series of bellwether, or test, trials whose outcomes are expected to guide the resolution of hundreds of similar lawsuits across the United States.

"We are proud to have achieved justice for our bellwether clients so far, including K.D.B. and S.J.," the lawyers said in a statement, referring to the plaintiffs, who are identified only by their initials.

"Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal."
Snap, the maker of Snapchat, said in a statement that it was "pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner."
Meta confirmed a settlement with KDB on Friday, after previously settling with SJ, which left Snap as the sole defendant in the case which consolidated claims from two lawsuits.
Sources close to Meta told AFP the company decided to settle for business reasons.
TikTok and YouTube were also named as defendants in the case, but both had already reached settlements as well.

Lawyers for SJ and KDB were expected to argue that their clients were exposed to "addictive and problematic" social media apps when they started using them at ages 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.
Twists and turns

Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.
The cases – the first of which went to trial earlier this year in Los Angeles – have taken twists and turns.

Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier this year, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined $6 million penalty.
Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.

Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August; that plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.
By settling before a trial kicks off, the social media companies contain costs from lawyer fees and potential penalties.
Another benefit is that it shields their executives from testifying in court or insider documents spilling into the public domain.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel had been expected to be called as key witnesses in the upcoming Los Angeles trial.

In August, Meta agreed to pay more than US$18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys general several days into a trial held in California.
That settlement came just a day after Mosseri testified, and before Zuckerberg had been called to the stand.
Meta has faced other trials, though.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
A New Mexico jury also found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of US$942 million earlier this year.
