a25d5f10bd8ee27e: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.

At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online.

Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out.

Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.

They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.

As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services.

Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not.

How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.”
Building a web for agents

There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers.

When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces.

The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not.
PINGNAN LU

So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do.

In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree.

Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information.

But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Salesforce.

Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.”

This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs.

As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly human-dominated web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book, Co-Existence, he decided to put together an agent-directed version that tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them.

In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents might end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had used an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code, and that hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes.

As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there.
The economics of control

Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote.

In an email to MIT Technology Review, an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer.

But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy.

Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026.

It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment.

E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up.

David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy.

Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees.

It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents.

When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.”

Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails.
The same can’t be said for OpenClaw.
“These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.”
How will the human web change?

When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile.

Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.”
“But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.”
PINGNAN LU
ec5375719a4d451b: VIENTIANE: Rising from verdant ridgelines of southern Laos, 133 Chinese-built wind turbines help power Vietnam's surging growth and represent part of a regional rush to diversify energy sources.
"The view is beautiful. They're bigger than trees," 23-year-old Toukta Phonsala told AFP inside her wooden stilt house in Dak Wai village, her baby bouncing on her lap.
Hydroelectric dams have proliferated across Southeast Asia in recent years, but production drops off in the dry season and critics lament the ecological impacts.
Experts say wind is now set to take off, and point to Laos's 600MW Monsoon Wind Power Project, which began operating in August 2025, as a bankable case study.
Spanning an area the size of Singapore, the approximately US$950-million scheme is the first cross-border wind project in Asia and the largest wind farm in Southeast Asia.
Built by a Chinese state firm and owned by a Thai-led consortium, it sells electricity exclusively to Vietnam's national grid via dedicated transmission lines.
Manufacturing hub Vietnam, Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, was already importing hydropower from Laos, its poorest neighbour.
However, "the economics are moving in favour of wind", said Tristan Bellingham, technical programme lead at nonprofit EnergyLab Asia.
"Similar to hydro 20 to 30 years ago, there's a bit of a rush on to secure concessions and development rights" for new wind projects, he told AFP.
Laos already hosts 90 hydropower plants and there are dozens more in neighbouring nations, leaving few optimal sites remaining.
'Better for development'
Bellingham said other wind farms were now riding "the coattails of Monsoon", with one Laos official pointing to 10 to 15 projects under development nationwide.
For Toukta, the 18 family members she lives with and other rice and coffee farmers residing near the turbines, Monsoon has brought new roads and improved access to fresh water and healthcare.
What it has not brought to her community, however, is power.
Residents say they still experience outages during heavy storms, as Laos's own electricity infrastructure is outdated and the state utility is heavily in debt.
Still, Toukta is glad Laos can send power abroad.
"It's better for development and can bring prosperity," she said.
For Vietnam, the project offers a reliable source of less costly energy.

There were severe blackouts in 2023 when drought cut into hydropower supply, and the government warned in September of the risk of electricity shortages from next year due to delays in planned power projects and increasing demand.
Through Monsoon, "wind power is being sold significantly cheaper to Vietnam than what Vietnam is buying wind power for locally", said Thomas Jakobsen, managing director at Indochina Energy Partners.
He estimated state utility Electricity Vietnam (EVN) was paying Monsoon around six cents per kilowatt-hour - two to four cents less than the Vietnamese rate.
Representatives of Monsoon Wind, EVN and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Monsoon project's financial arranger, declined to share the rate during a press tour last week.
'Something unique'
The project is also key to Vietnam reaching net-zero emissions targets by 2050, according to Ninh Xuan Hiep, an official at EVN's National Power Transmission Corporation.
At a substation in the Vietnamese capital Hanoi, he told AFP that by 2030, Laos imports would equal nearly 10 percent of Vietnam's total installed capacity - its maximum possible production.
Monsoon Wind plans to boost capacity by 1,000 megawatts and is working to ensure some of this additional power is used inside Laos, according to general manager Narut Boakajorn.
"Laos has so much natural resources" - wind, hydro and solar, Narut told AFP in an interview held below the spinning blades of a 110-metre-high turbine.
"Not many countries have all the good renewable energy in the same place. Laos has something unique," Narut said.
The government was set to reap US$180 million over the 25-year contract period, including taxes and community development and environmental protection funds, according to Narut.
He insisted nobody was forced to relocate because of the project - although public dissent is severely restricted in communist Laos.
He said 1,600 grievances logged, mainly from farmers requesting compensation for construction impacts on their crops, were resolved.
In the shadow of the turbines, 23-year-old farmer Phonekhan Sengsopha said he was proud that electricity produced in his country was being sent to its neighbour, also a communist nation.
"Because Vietnam and Laos are like brothers. They help one another," Sengsopha said.
ca2f4f22b33f45bc: As robotaxis continue trials in London, an independent research group thinks the UK needs to answer some serious questions before heading any further down the road.

To kick off, the sovereignty question, or "Will Britain become dependent on autonomous vehicle services for any key activities and what fallback options will exist if a supplier fails or withdraws?" as the Institute for Driverless Transport (IfDT) puts it.

Another question concerns employment: "To what extent does professional driving form part of the UK's employment safety net and how will this function be recreated if demand for professional drivers is significantly reduced?"

The objective for IfDT — an independent UK research and convening body focused on the consequences of autonomous vehicles — is to cast the net a bit wider than simply thinking about whether the software is sufficient to navigate London’s wiggly streets and narrow alleys.

The research draws on work with operators trying to bring AVs to London and the regulators responsible for policy. It also relied on more than 30 conversations with councils, operators, industry, unions, charities, insurers, lawyers and universities.

James Hutt, IfDT co-founder, said: "What struck us most in the interviews was how far this reaches: into jobs, public services, the built environment and national resilience. The people who know those areas best are rarely part of the conversation about AVs.

"Our next step is to bring funding and researchers together with the businesses and public bodies that need answers. If you can fund research or offer a place to test it, we would like to hear from you."
In August, Transport for London (TfL) granted private hire licences to autonomous vehicle operators provided that a human driver is present during journeys.
Wayve and Uber have since launched self-driving rides in the UK capital, with 15 electric Ford Mustangs, equipped with the Wayve AI driver, set to pick up passengers with a safety driver on board.
UK company Wayve also demoed a Nissan LEAF, running the Wayve AI Driver using NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion with self-driving equipment built more closely into the car's design.
IfDT points out that Waymo and Baidu are also preparing services for London, while Uber, Pony.ai and Verne have begun testing in Manchester.

The research organization said UK authorities still need to answer a long list of questions in order to shape long-term infrastructure plans for local areas and prepare for AI's impact on the labor market.
The question of who needs to do this also remains unanswered, as the IfDT asks:
"Which are the key public bodies that should already be anticipating the impact of AVs on their own work and who within those organisations should lead a response?"®
2f9eda7ddfe33f5e: ABU DHABI, Nov 2 — UAE state oil company ADNOC today announced a partnership with OpenAI, saying it would be the world’s first energy firm to deploy OpenAI Frontier, an advanced artificial intelligence platform.

The deal was announced as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman attended the UAE’s flagship oil industry event in Abu Dhabi, which has bet heavily on the technology in a bid to diversify its economy away from energy.
Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, but the US military has been escorting ships through the route.
The blockade has caused a spike in oil prices.
ADNOC said in a statement that OpenAI’s models will enable it to to be “the first energy company in the world to use this technology to value every barrel while it is still in the ground”.
The deal will also see ADNOC and OpenAI partner with G42, and Emirati AI company chaired by the brother of the UAE’s president.
The oil-rich UAE is a top AI player in the Middle East and has been seeking to become a dominant force in the field globally.

“From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI, and now together we will find out what AI can do for energy,” said ADNOC’s managing director and CEO Sultan Al Jaber at the ADIPEC oil conference.
Altman praised the UAE as having “consistently been the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”.

According to an ADNOC statement, “OpenAI’s advanced reasoning models will integrate decades of data across thousands of wells, multiple stacked reservoirs and hundreds of surface facilities together with capital, cost and commercial considerations, to prepare and optimise full-field development master plans”.

“Interconnected AI agents will continuously forecast crude oil supply, demand, prices and margins, predict their impacts before they occur, and weigh the commercial and operational impact of every decision as one integrated process,” the statement said.
No financial details of the deal were disclosed.
The UAE has been betting heavily on AI since 2017, when it named the world’s first AI minister and became the second country after Canada to unveil a national AI strategy.

A year later, G42 was founded with backing from Abu Dhabi-based sovereign wealth fund Mubadala. Chaired by the UAE president’s brother, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, it offers a range of AI products and employs more than 23,000 people.
Last year, intense lobbying bore fruit when the US approved the export of advanced Nvidia chips to both the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Yesterday, Saudi state oil firm Aramco said it was taking a 49 per cent stake in Saudi state-backed AI company Humain, injecting cash and assets as the tech firm tries to scale up to meet rising demand.

b9f5c6ab743c9e01: Nanjing Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. (NISCO) has worked with Huawei and ecosystem partners to commercially deploy the world's first steel model powered by swarm intelligence - the YuanYe Steel Large Model (YuanYe) - across multiple scenarios at scale. This helps NISCO transition its core operations from relying on experience to being powered by data and intelligence collaboration.

As a traditional manufacturer navigating the challenges of transformation and cost efficiency, NISCO has built a robust digital and intelligent foundation by adopting industry-leading products including Ascend, Kunpeng, Huawei Cloud Stack, and Pangu models. By embedding AI into every core stage of production - ironmaking, steelmaking, rolling, and quality inspection - NISCO is forging green and high-end AI-powered super steel plants.

Unlike general-purpose monolithic models, YuanYe innovatively fuses multiple AI models with the steel industry's metallurgical mechanism models to create a dual-drive, multi-model cluster architecture. This architecture features a "right brain" for probabilistic computing and a "left brain" for precise and scientific decision-making. Powered by massive amounts of sensing data aggregated from millions of operational technology (OT) data points across 26 business domains, NISCO has achieved real-time digital twin mapping within its intelligent operations center, laying solid data and scenario foundations for YuanYe. This enables the entire steelmaking process to become not only visible, but also capable of precise control and intelligent assessment. Now 100 percent of NISCO's key equipment is connected and digitally controlled and its new product R&D cycles have been shortened by 50 percent, reducing annual costs by over CNY100m (approx. US$15m).

As the model continues to iterate, NISCO had launched 25 business agents by October 2026. These agents cover a wide range of scenarios, from visual quality inspection and process optimization to production scheduling and operations management, setting a new benchmark for digital and intelligent steel transformation.
Breakthroughs in four core scenarios: YuanYe redefines traditional operations for significant safety, efficiency, and quality gains

In the ironmaking stage, AI makes traditionally invisible blast furnaces transparent. YuanYe leverages blast furnaces' internal sensor data and metallurgical mechanism analysis to perform real-time dynamic simulations of the ironmaking process. Assisted by furnace temperature prediction and health diagnosis models, furnace operators can predict temperatures and identify issues two hours in advance, with over 90 percent accuracy. This shifts furnace operations from reactive post-event remediation to proactive pre-control, increasing prime-grade molten iron yield by over 10 percent while significantly cutting unit energy consumption.

In the rolling stage, AI drives precise predictions and codifies expert experience to enhance the operational stability of steel rolling and secure leadership in product quality. To tackle the highly dynamic and complex operating conditions during the rolling process, YuanYe's rolling-force prediction model achieves millisecond-level response, narrowing the thickness tolerance to ±0.2 mm and reducing the steel thickness deviation to 1.9 percent to reach a world-leading standard. The rolling-force hit rate has jumped from 88 percent to 98 percent, supporting a steady annual output of over 2.5 million tons of steel plates and increasing the overall yield rate by 0.5 percent. Enhanced dimensional precision and physical-chemical stability allow NISCO's products to meet demanding steel specifications across diverse applications, ranging from mega stadiums and oil pipelines to 10,000-ton cruise ships and LNG storage tanks.

In quality inspection, the synergy between robots and AI models serves as a discerning "eagle eye", doubling metallographic inspection efficiency. During metallographic inspection for finished steel, the integrated smart metallographic inspection system built on YuanYe has achieved full-process automation, covering sample grinding and polishing, image acquisition, and smart grading. Inspection accuracy has risen to over 95 percent, while per-sample inspection time has been shortened from 10 minutes down to 3–5 minutes. This 80 percent increase in overall inspection efficiency frees human operators to focus on anomaly analysis and high-level decision-making.

In the energy and environmental control stage, NISCO leverages the YuanYe architecture to develop the S-Link Intelligent Agent for Gas and Flue Gas Sulfur Control. Integrating 602 process parameters alongside multi-modal image and knowledge capabilities, the agent achieves a smart closed loop across source prediction, process optimization, and end-of-pipe compliance. By combining mechanism inversion with time-series forecasting, it issues precise sulfur-risk warnings one hour in advance, achieving a sulfur prediction accuracy of over 95 percent. Operational optimization algorithms then calculate the optimal gas blending scheme within seconds. Finally, game-theoretic models dynamically allocate emission quotas, slashing natural gas co-firing consumption by nearly 50 percent. This has reduced downtime caused by emission exceedance by over 25 percent, and delivered more than CNY600,000 (approx. US$90,000) in annual economic benefits - securing both environmental compliance and drastic cost reduction.
From automating labor to empowering people: Defining a new paradigm of inclusive AI

Li Jinyan, General Manager of the Digital and Intelligent Integrated Development Department and Director of the AI Research Institute at NISCO, said: "Digital and intelligent transformation is inherently human-centric. Its purpose is not to replace people, but to unleash human potential. Our goal is to lift employees out of the endless sea of data, empowering them to direct their creative energy toward work of higher value." To date, NISCO has deployed over 300 AI models across its plants, alongside more than 1,000 low-code agents and lightweight applications built independently by frontline employees.

As Cheng Yongfu, Senior Industrial Solution Expert at Huawei's Steel & Non-ferrous BU, noted: "The real value of industrial AI can only be realized when it expands from single-point applications to comprehensive integration with production, operations, and management, which can unlock sustained, scalable empowerment."

Looking ahead, as model deployment expands and computing demands continue to grow, NISCO will team up with Huawei and other partners to explore the construction of dedicated data centers for smart steel plants. Centered on the AI-native three-tier architecture (AI-native OS, AI-native factory, and AI-native enterprise) and powered by the YuanYe model, NISCO is accelerating high-quality steel development, aiming to provide a replicable and scalable benchmark for the digital and intelligent transformation of the global steel and manufacturing industries.

6a62b628a03d80c8: From Ashraf Abdullah
Moaz Nair’s “Bedfellows and backstabbers on the winding road to Putrajaya” mistakes colourful language for a convincing explanation of Malaysian politics.

His argument rests on two questionable assumptions: that cooperation in the federal government requires permanent electoral allegiance, and that the next general election is guaranteed to produce a hung Parliament.
Neither should pass unchallenged.
The unity government emerged after GE15 in November 2022, when no coalition secured a parliamentary majority.

The 16th Yang di-Pertuan Agong urged political cooperation to resolve the impasse. Umno’s supreme council subsequently supported its participation in a unity government, specifying that it should not be led by Perikatan Nasional.

That context matters. Barisan Nasional (BN) helped establish a functioning administration following an inconclusive election. It did not merge with Pakatan Harapan (PH) or surrender its political identity.

Supporting an administration during a parliamentary term and deciding whom to contest alongside at the next election are distinct decisions. Describing that distinction as “backstabbing” requires more than metaphors about political bedrooms.

For accuracy, BN’s leadership has previously advocated extending cooperation into GE16. In June 2024, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said BN would maintain cooperation with PH while contesting under its own symbol. That statement cannot simply be erased from the record.
But neither can it be treated as an irrevocable undertaking regardless of subsequent developments.
In January this year, Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the party had not decided whether cooperation with PH would continue at GE16.

More recently, Zahid reaffirmed BN’s commitment to the unity government until the end of the present Parliament. These statements underline why the governing commitment, and future electoral arrangements must be examined separately.

Zahid’s preference alone should not determine BN’s electoral future. As Umno president and BN chairman, he must secure support within his party and take into account the positions of other BN component parties.

Umno members, its decision-making bodies, MCA and MIC have interests and constituencies of their own. An arrangement affecting their survival requires collective backing. Leadership involves listening to those whom one leads. And lest we forget, BN makes decisions by consensus.
It must also involve listening to voters.
In my assessment, continued electoral cooperation with PH will be increasingly difficult to sell to voters frustrated by promises which remain unfulfilled.
PH campaigned on reform and better governance. Its supporters are entitled to judge the delivery against the expectations its leaders created.

BN cannot assume that those frustrations are somebody else’s problem. Sharing power also means sharing public scrutiny. Ignoring discontent to preserve an understanding between leaders could prove costly at the ballot box.

Resistance among many Malay voters to cooperation with DAP presents another challenge. This does not mean every Malay voter thinks alike, or that election results establish a single reason for voting.
They do, however, require BN to examine whether its present partnership helps recover traditional supporters or pushes them further away.

Nair’s treatment of Umno and PAS is heavy with derision. I find considerable venom in his descriptions of Umno and PAS in this particular article and in his past jottings, perhaps because both are Malay-based parties.
He makes little effort to understand the constituencies these parties represent. Their supporters deserve analysis rather than caricature.
The election evidence also deserves more attention than his confident prediction allows.

In Sabah’s November 2025 election, DAP failed to win any of the eight seats it contested. Its secretary-general Loke Siew Fook accepted responsibility. Much of the electoral benefit went to Warisan, illustrating that dissatisfaction with DAP need not translate automatically into support for MCA.
Nevertheless, the warning was unmistakable: established support cannot be taken for granted.
Johor delivered another forceful reminder. In the July 2026 state election, BN won 48 of 56 seats, including eight won by MCA. PH secured eight seats, six through DAP. PN failed to win a seat.
Those results demonstrate both BN’s renewed strength and the danger of assuming that any party possesses an unassailable electoral base.

An analysis by the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, part of Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore identified declining Chinese support for PH alongside weaker turnout in its urban strongholds.
Its estimates still placed most Chinese voters with PH but showed meaningful erosion. A party need not lose an entire community’s support to lose constituencies where the contest is close.
Some voters may choose MCA. Others may abstain. Neither response guarantees a particular national outcome, but both can alter electoral arithmetic.

Negeri Sembilan offers a different, equally relevant lesson. BN won 18 seats, PN seven and PH 11 in its August election. BN and PN therefore held 25 of the assembly’s 36 seats between them. Cooperation mattered to the resulting balance of power.

It would nevertheless be inaccurate to describe that result as proof of a wholesale Chinese rejection of PH. Bridget Welsh’s analysis estimated that Chinese support remained overwhelmingly with PH. The stronger argument concerns the combination of constituency results and cooperation between competing political forces.
Together, these elections challenge the notion that PH’s position is secure or that fragmentation must inevitably produce another hung Parliament.
My assessment is that an effective BN-PN electoral understanding could win a comfortable parliamentary majority.
Avoiding mutually damaging contests, consolidating overlapping support and recovering some non-Malay votes offer a credible route to that outcome.

That remains a forecast. Seat negotiations, candidates, turnout and the positions of Sabah and Sarawak parties will matter. But Nair cannot reasonably demand certainty from competing scenarios while presenting his own as guaranteed.

He should visit Melaka and take the pulse of the campaign. BN is contesting 23 seats and PN five. Zahid has publicly said BN would invite successful PN assemblymen into the administration if it forms the government. This is an openly stated political understanding, not a clandestine affair.
Melaka votes on Nov 14. Its verdict remains with the electorate.
Cooperation in government does not confer permanent ownership over a partner’s electoral choices.
Changed arrangements require explanation, but they do not automatically establish betrayal.
The road to Putrajaya may be winding but a hung Parliament, to my mind, is not a foregone conclusion, like Nair confidently puts it.
The writer is a former group managing editor of Media Prima Bhd’s Television Networks.

0bcd54b5cef9c5b8: Welcome to Monday morning, an occasion The Register marks with a new instalment of "Who, Me?" It's our reader-contributed column in which you confess to workplace mistakes and share your escapes from subsequent scrapes.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Gordon" who told us he once worked as an engineer at a major semiconductor corporation.

Gordon rose to become manager of an engineering team which worked on a very popular PC chipset. One of the chaps on this team wasn't pulling his weight, so Gordon got the job of telling him to improve, or leave.
"In all fairness, he was a nice guy but not a great engineer and needed to be better," Gordon told The Register.

Not long after that moment of managerial unpleasantness, Gordon's team got the job of doing a full backup of the chipset's "production stepping" – the silicon equivalent of a minor point release. The idea was to create a detailed record that could be used as a restore point.

"This was not a nightly backup, but a purposeful backup to retain a snapshot of the entire cleaned-up design database for future cases where we might need to spin another stepping quickly," Gordon explained.
Gordon told his underperforming colleague to do the backup. "Because I was overworked, I did not think this through," he told The Register.
The at-risk worker quickly proved why he was under the pump by deciding the backup wasn't necessary until the team completed the next stepping – but didn't tell anyone about that plan.
Before that next stepping was done, the employee's past indiscretions caught up with him and he was let go.
The story now fast-forwards six years, to a moment when Gordon learned that a customer wanted to buy the old chipset design so they could make a radiation-hardened version to use on satellites.
The major semiconductor company liked the sound of that, and asked Gordon to find the backup.

"My colleague and I then pieced together what had happened," he wrote. "Being good engineers, we said nothing. We searched through old nightly backup tapes until we found bits and pieces of different steppings of the design database and copied them all to one place, then handed this off to the customer."
To this day, Gordon doesn't know if the customer was able to produce a useful chip from the bits of backup he cobbled together.
"Did they realize they received bits and pieces of two slightly different databases? Did they care? Was the project canceled before anyone realized it?"

"From then on, I was more careful about who I assigned the task of creating restore backups for each design project," he told The Register. "And I kept a record of the emails requesting backups and confirmation that backups had been done."
Have you given a job to the wrong person? Or given clients slightly dodgy data? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We would love to tell your tale on a future Monday. ®

0cacd9e7aeeb24e0: A designer named Marcin Wichary has revealed the story of how he freaked out a decent slab of the world’s Firefox-using population with Pac-Man.

Wichary has held senior design roles at Figma, Medium, and Google. As he wrote here, in 2010 Google decided to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Pac-Man by changing its logo at Google.com to a playable version of the game.

The Google of 2010 could still mention its motto of the time, “Don’t be evil,” without making anyone who heard it guffaw incredulously. The company’s frequent changes to the logo on its homepage – called Google Doodles, and which persist to this day – were still a notable part of net culture.
Wichary got the job of building the playable logo, and tweaking Pac-Man to replace its usual maze with a course that instead navigated around the letters GOOGLE.

“It was, frankly, a terrifying proposition,” Wichary wrote. “The homepage was then a very important destination, and my job title was only adjacent to ‘software engineer.’ But I started researching the game and recreating it all in HTML and CSS."
Google wanted a full Pac-Man experience, including sound, "because so many of Pac-Man’s sounds are beyond iconic: the starting melody, the waka-wakas, the death jingle."
Wichary began work before Google sought permission from Pac-Man’s owner Namco, because the search giant was “planning to wow them with a close-to-finished doodle.”
“The project was … going really well. I had fun coding the game and we seemed to have fun playing it. Namco eventually got onboard, too,” he wrote.
Google liked the game work so much, higher-ups decided it would be a great idea to have it start automatically if visitors to google.com stayed idle for ten seconds.

The designer liked that idea. “If there was anything scary about it at the time, it was only the thought of my code getting even more exposure – but I wasn’t worried about distraction, since the homepage was not a destination page you would ever linger on.”
What Google didn’t realise was that some people lingered on the home page without ever knowing they were there.
Those people used the Firefox browser with an extension called CoolPreviews that let users hover over a link to see a preview of a web page.
“The extension would quietly start at the same time Firefox was opened,” Wichary explained. “And it would immediately, in the background, invisibly and unbeknownst to the user, open a website.”
That website was Google’s home page, which now featured an auto-playing and version of Pac-Man that CoolPreviews users simply did not expect.

Which explained why, not long after setting the Pac-Man doodle live, Google received plenty of praise, but also reports about computers making strange noises due to CoolPreviews invisibly opening the noisy game.

“I pushed a patch within hours,” Wichary wrote, explaining that he added a mute button and a requirement to click something to make the game and its noises start. CoolPreviews couldn’t make those clicks, so the phantom Pac-Man sounds went away.

“Ironically, I don’t believe we ever heard of normal people being bothered by the autoplay – it seemed that indeed, few people stayed on the homepage for 10 seconds doing absolutely nothing,” Wichary wrote.

“The funny thing is that emergency live-patching [the] internet’s at the time most valuable homepage was perhaps the scariest part of that day for me, but that completely went over my sleep-deprived head,” he added.
Google changed Wichary’s title after this incident. His post shows an image describing him as “User experience designer. The Michael Bay of doodles.” ®

624e23d0cdf0ab77: Regina Barzilay, MIT’s School of Engineering Distinguished Professor of AI and Health, and James Collins, MIT’s Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering and Science, are the recipients of the 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence.  The award recognizes their joint work in “pioneering AI-enabled antibiotic discovery, integrating deep learning, bioengineering, and experimental validation to identify novel antibacterial candidates against drug-resistant pathogens.”  Established in 2024 by the University of Chicago in partnership with Caltech, the Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence recognizes contributions that jointly advance AI and the natural sciences or engineering. Barzilay and Collins, who are faculty co-leads of the Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and affiliates of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing and the MIT School of Engineering, published their first breakthrough paper together in 2020 with then-MIT postdoc and first author Jonathan Stokes (who worked in the Collins lab from 2017 to 2021) in Cell. The paper described the first artificial intelligence-discovered antibiotic, called halicin, named for the fictional AI system HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey. A broad-spectrum antibiotic that was originally studied as a potential diabetes drug, halicin was identified by a deep learning model trained on 2,500 molecules. Upon testing, the research team found that halicin was able to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria (i.e., “superbugs”) such as Clostridium difficile, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A discovery process that once took years was completed in just a few weeks. Amidst the growing alarm around the global antimicrobial resistance crisis, the results demonstrated that AI could prove to be an effective tool for rapidly identifying new and effective antibiotics. Following halicin, Barzilay and Collins worked with Stokes (now an assistant professor at McMaster University) to use machine learning to identify abaucin in 2023, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic demonstrating effectiveness against A. baumannii, an antibiotic-resistant bacteria commonly found on hospital doorknobs and in the wounds of U.S. soldiers stationed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Notably, abaucin’s “narrow spectrum” efficacy against a single species of treatment-resistant bacteria is its main advantage, minimizing the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance and harming beneficial bacteria in the gut. “Historically, antibiotic discovery has depended on laborious, trial-and-error strategies,” says Collins. “This process is slow, costly, and unpredictable, often yielding few viable antibiotic candidates. With generative AI, we're now seeing a shift from AI being used as a tool for discovery to AI being used as a design tool. This shift opens new frontiers in antibiotic discovery that could bring us the next generation of lifesaving drugs.” In Barzilay’s view, “despite significant progress in molecular modeling, we are still in early stages of drug discovery. With AI, we can only automate parts of the pipeline, rather than totally transforming the discovery process. To make it happen, we need to work really hard to build realistic AI models of human biology.”

7a7101b3da478fc1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — Malaysian factories are wrestling with mounting transport and material bills, passing these higher overheads directly to buyers as factory-gate inflation matches rising production costs.

According to the latest S&P Global Malaysia Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI), input expenses and selling charges rose at identical, accelerated rates in October. Survey respondents pinned the surge in freight and raw material expenses partly on ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Despite intensifying cost burdens, overall sector performance returned to expansion territory. The headline PMI climbed to 51.0 in October from 49.9 in September, crossing the 50-point threshold separating contraction from growth to mark its strongest showing since April.

New orders surged at one of the fastest paces seen in four and a half years, driven by robust export sales and renewed demand from existing domestic clients. That rebound prompted factories to lift output for the first time in three months and expand headcount for a third consecutive month.
“New orders returned to growth, supported in part by stronger demand for AI-related products, and underpinned a fresh rise in output,” S&P Global economist Maryam Baluch said in the report.
Supply snags and port congestion persist

Operational bottlenecks continue to restrain the sector's recovery. Delivery schedules for manufacturing inputs deteriorated for an eleventh straight month, with chronic port congestion singled out as a recurring headache, even though delays eased marginally compared to September.
To keep pace with rising order books, several factories tapped into existing stockpiles, drawing down finished goods inventories for a sixth consecutive month.

Yet the turnaround in orders and output did little to lift long-term sentiment. Business confidence slumped to its lowest level since April, a mood the survey characterised as historically subdued. Manufacturers cited escalating expenses alongside broad geopolitical and macroeconomic volatility as reasons for caution.
Baluch noted that external headwinds remain “a key threat to the economy’s current resilience.”

While the PMI measures factory-gate prices rather than retail shop tags, the rapid pass-through of expenses from manufacturers to intermediate buyers signals potential inflationary pressure downstream that could eventually filter through to consumers.
The survey reflects responses collected between October 12 and 26 from purchasing managers across approximately 400 manufacturing operations in Malaysia.

7feeedd4d2bf32cd: From Moaz Nair
Welcome to the era of "polytropous" politics, a term analysts use when they want to politely say our politicians suffer from severe relationship commitment issues.

As we barrel towards the 16th general election, the political landscape in the Peninsula resembles less a stable Westminster democracy and more a chaotic, high-stakes episode of "The Bachelor: Putrajaya Edition".
For those trying to keep track of the prospective political mathematics, the current options on Anwar Ibrahim’s whiteboard read like labels on a broken calculator:
Pakatan Harapan Plus, Perikatan Nasional Plus, or perhaps a convoluted equation like Barisan Nasional-minus-Bersatu, Wawasan, Gerakan, Malaysian Indian People’s Party, and Pejuang, multiplied by PAS.
The truth is, no one has locked in a mega-coalition because everyone is too busy playing the field.

Take Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, the grand master of political gymnastics. At the federal level, the Umno president sits snugly in the marital bed of the unity government with PH and the DAP, smiling warmly for the cameras.
But the moment he crosses state borders into Johor, Negeri Sembilan, or the electoral war zone of Melaka, Zahid sneaks out the back window to hook up with Abdul Hadi Awang and PAS.
Talk about a shameless double life. Zahid and Anwar run the country together during the week, but come the weekend, BN teams up with PAS to try and wipe PH off the state map.

When launching the Melaka election machinery, Zahid proudly declared that "hijau sudah menerima biru" (green has accepted blue). Yet the irony is loud: BN aggressively kept 23 seats for itself, dumping the remaining five hard-to-win seats on PAS and its PN allies.
But let’s be real — this romance has a strict ceiling.

Zahid wants PAS and PAS only, completely blanking other PN roommates. Besides, is Hadi really going to hand over safe seats in Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah, or Perlis just to be nice to Umno? Local warlords say there's a better chance of snow hitting these states, especially after Umno just squeezed their allies out of two extra seats in Melaka.
PN is trapped

Meanwhile, PN is trapped in a dilemma of its own making. To properly court BN, they are being asked to dump their entire entourage — Gerakan, MIPP, Pejuang, and the newly minted Wawasan led by the exiled Hamzah Zainudin. It turns out Zahid doesn't want to pay for a group dinner.
To make matters funnier, the house that Gerakan and MIPP are clinging to is literally on fire.

In a massive political shockwave on Oct 20, the Registrar of Societies officially cancelled Perikatan Nasional's registration. This stemmed from a toxic internal feud where Bersatu complained it was unlawfully excluded from a crucial PN council meeting. Though the High Court granted a temporary stay on Oct 22, the alliance is legally a "ghost ship" caught in intense friction, while its internal engine — Bersatu under Muhyiddin Yassin — is causing an absolute earthquake of instability.

Naturally, the vacuum has sparked wild rumours. Whisper it, in Shah Alam, but word on the street is that a fractured Bersatu is looking to jump ship entirely and work with PH, starting with a cosy trial marriage in Selangor that could spread nationwide.

This comes hot on the heels of party leaders executing a federal confidence and supply agreement with Anwar Ibrahim’s government — a pact explicitly designed to buy parliamentary stability and secure the passage of the 2027 budget.
If you're keeping score: Zahid is sleeping with PN's partner, while Muhyiddin's remnants are trying to move in with Zahid's federal spouse.

While the Peninsula fractures into a million messy social media threads, East Malaysia is watching the soap opera with mild amusement. The regional titans, Gabungan Parti Sarawak and Gabungan Rakyat Sabah have zero interest in joining a rigid, peninsula-centric bloc or any stressful mega-coalition.
Why buy into the drama now when you can just sit back, secure your own backyard, and wait to play kingmaker after the election?
It's complicated

When the dust settles on GE16, the only guaranteed result is of a spectacularly hung parliament. None of the party leaders, Anwar, Zahid, Muhyiddin, and Hadi, will have the 112-seat magic number to form a government on their own. We won't see clean "plus" coalitions on the ballot paper.

Instead, we will get "fluid understandings"— the political equivalent of "it's complicated". Our leaders will avoid three-cornered fights where convenient, stab each other in the back where necessary, and then awkwardly gather in a hotel ballroom post-election to figure out who hates each other the least.
Brace yourselves. The road to Putrajaya is no longer a highway; it’s a swinging party, and everyone is invited.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

8d8227e52875b593: In 1968, Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich opened his book The Population Bomb with a sentence that still makes me wince: "The battle to feed all of humanity is over." In the 1970s, he predicted, "hundreds of millions of people will starve to death", no matter what crash programmes we launched.

Instead came the Green Revolution, and between 1960 and 2005 the yields of major cereal crops more than doubled while real food prices fell by over 50%. Yet when a New York Times documentary series asked him about the book in 2015, Ehrlich, who died in March at 93, replied: "My language would be even more apocalyptic today."

I can't help but feel we are watching the same film again, except that this time the bomb is AI. And here's the kicker: the people who understand it best are far less frightened of it than the rest of us.

When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans in 2024, 51% said they were more concerned than excited about AI, against a mere 15% of the 1,013 AI experts it polled. More than half of those experts, 56%, expected AI to have a positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years, compared with just 17% of the public.

Malaysians, refreshingly, haven't quite caught the bug. In market research firm Ipsos' 2025 survey of 30 countries, 77% of us said AI excites us, the third highest of the lot, though 55% admitted it also makes us nervous.

Now, I'm no doe-eyed optimist. In July, during an internal hacking test, roughly 700 of OpenAI's AI agents found exposed login credentials and broke into the servers of Hugging Face, an outside AI hosting company, and investigators found that the agents knew "this activity was out of scope and unethical", but joined in anyway.

Closer to home, by August 2024 the police's Commercial Crime Investigation Department was already probing 454 scams believed to involve deepfakes, AI-generated fake voices and videos, with RM2.72 million lost. And 63% of Malaysians worry that AI could take their job within the next three to five years.
These are grave dangers, which is exactly why we must build the brakes as we go. But a danger is not a destiny, and the odds, according to the researchers building this technology, are in our favour.

In a survey conducted in late 2023, 2,778 researchers who had published at top AI conferences and journals put the median chance of an extremely bad outcome, such as human extinction, at 5%. That's not nothing, but 68.3% of them said good outcomes were more likely than bad ones.
So what does the good outcome look like? We don't have to imagine it, because much of it is already here:
● Google DeepMind's AlphaFold mapped over 200 million protein shapes, earning its creators a Nobel Prize;
● AI-assisted screening of Swedish women caught 29% more breast cancers, with 44% less radiologist work;
● An AI at University of California San Diego cut hospital sepsis deaths by 17%; and
● A generative AI assistant lifted customer support productivity by 14%, and that of novice workers by 34%

That last point matters to anyone worried about their job, because the tool helped the least experienced workers the most, narrowing the gap between the rookie and the veteran rather than widening it. Just this week, Microsoft said its diagnostic AI correctly diagnosed 83% of complex medical cases against 36% for generalist doctors in a study published in the journal Science, though it has yet to be tested against specialists or on real patients.

And it's already at work in our own public health system. Dr Mata, an AI developed by the Ministry of Health with private firm Qmed Asia, screens diabetics for retinopathy, a leading cause of preventable blindness here, in about 30 seconds, in a country where 15.6% of adults have type 2 diabetes.

Meanwhile, seven government clinics, from Kajang in Selangor to Kok Lanas in Kelantan, were picked last year to pilot AI-assisted chest X-rays designed to catch lung disease earlier, at a one-off software cost of about RM10,000 per clinic.

Where does it go from here? Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who runs Google DeepMind, told CBS's 60 Minutes last year that ending all disease is "within reach. Maybe within the next decade or so, I don't see why not", before asking in the same interview: "Can we make sure that we can keep control of the systems?"
That is precisely the right posture, eyes wide open to the risks but feet firmly moving towards the reward. Fear has its uses, but it makes a terrible driver.

So by all means build the brakes, fund the police's deepfake hunters and retrain the workers whose jobs will change. But the next time someone tells you the battle for humanity's future is already lost, remember the global famine that never came, and the AI our own health ministry helped build that can now screen a diabetic's eyes in 30 seconds.

“For us, the broader opportunity is to develop a more mature used-EV ecosystem here, where vehicles can be assessed consistently and safely, and buyers have greater confidence in the condition of the cars they purchase,” Teoh was quoted as saying.

9cc4007b9998adb2: In a politically polarised American electorate, it can be hard to find bipartisan consensus on many issues. Ahead of the US midterm elections, however, there is one thing almost everyone can agree on: concern about government corruption. A record 89% of Americans recently said in a Gallup poll that government corruption is widespread, with Republicans, Democrats and independents all in agreement (ranging between 83-91%). This marks a significant increase from 73% in Gallup’s polling from 2024. Out of 132 countries Gallup polled on the question since 2023, only four have recorded higher overall levels of concern: Lebanon and Peru (both 92%), and Ghana and Nigeria (both 90%). As much as cost of living issues have defined much of the recent campaign rhetoric, a recent Fox News Poll found that concern about corruption in government (88%) ranked higher among voters than inflation (85%) or gas prices (83%). A CNBC survey similarly found government corruption to be the most important issue facing the country, above any concerns about the economy. And according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, of the US$11.6 billion that will be spent in political advertising this election cycle, more than US$275 million has gone to corruption-themed ads – around US$173 for Democrats and US$93 for Republicans. An ad produced by a Democratic super PAC accusing Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins of corruption. An ad by Republican Minnesota Senate candidate Michele Tafoya accusing Democrats of failing to stop fraud in the state. Who do Americans blame? As much as Democrats point to the unprecedented gifts from foreign governments to the Trump family and the massive expansion of the Trump family wealth during Donald Trump’s second presidential term, Americans are by no means exclusively blaming the Trump administration for corruption. When the Brennan Center for Justice, a voting rights organisation, asked a representative sample of 2,000 Americans this year whether certain individuals or institutions were corrupt, respondents had negative views across the political spectrum. These included view about Congress (85%), Trump (68%), Joe Biden (63%) and the Supreme Court (62%). And when asked whether this is a problem driven by individuals making unethical choices or a problem “deeply embedded in the institutions of the US government”, about two-thirds of respondents chose the latter. Only 7% said they were not concerned about corruption influencing elected officials. This does not appear to be a new phenomenon. Levels of trust in American politicians, political parties, news media, government institutions and even the “American people” have been declining since Gallup began polling on the issue in the 1970s. And they’ve hit record lows in recent years. While 86% of Americans trusted the American people in 1976, today barely half do. Adding further nuance to this issue: Gallup also highlights the significant gap between American perceptions of corruption in government (89%) versus corruption in business (71%). The survey says few countries have gaps this large. And, interestingly, this public perception of corruption does not trickle down to local politics. In another survey by YouGov many more respondents deemed US senators and representatives to be corrupt (75%) than mid- or low-level government workers (39%). This gets to an important reason why such high levels of distrust in institutions have not led to more unrest: Americans still appear to have trust in their local governments. And this has largely not changed since Gallup first polled on the topic more than 50 years ago. Today, two-thirds of Americans trust their local government, which is actually slightly higher than the 63% who did in 1972. On the whole, Americans also retain trust in the ability of elections – like the midterms – to act as political circuit breakers. What about the midterms? Candidates running for office this year have taken note of the deep voter distrust in Washington elites, parties and institutions. One need only watch a few of the many viral political ads this campaign to see a well-worn script: candidates blame Washington insiders for corruption and other issues, while touting their local bona fides. It should come as no surprise that many candidates are eschewing party labels altogether, often going so far as to criticise their own party. But this is not the first time politicians of all stripes have appeared keen to distance themselves from the ruling class, and from political insiders viewed as corrupt and detached from the everyday realities of most Americans. After all, with the exceptions of Biden and George H.W. Bush (both former vice presidents who served under popular two-term presidents), every US president of the last half century has come to the Oval Office with fewer than five years of experience in Washington – if any. Americans have largely been against Washington insiders for decades – particularly when economic anxiety is high. Yet what’s different in this year’s midterm elections is how many are trying to fuse corruption with that economic anxiety. Not since the 2006 midterm elections has corruption been such a prominent theme in an election. James Talarico, the Democratic hopeful for the Senate in Texas, has said on the campaign trail, “we have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis”. And in Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff routinely tells voters “corruption is why things don’t work for ordinary people.” Talarico ad accusing his opponent of being the ‘most corrupt politician in Texas’. Ossoff ad linking corruption to cost-of-living issues for Americans. These Democratic efforts follow similar efforts by Republicans to portray Democrats as the more corrupt party costing American taxpayers money. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, for instance, sought to target what it called “waste, fraud and abuse”. And Republicans in Minnesota have highlighted a welfare-fraud scandal that essentially forced Democratic Governor Tim Walz to abandon his plans for a third term of office. Ad by Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson alleging corruption by his Democratic opponent. It’s unclear whether these sorts of accusations will inspire the political backlash that other issues – namely abortion, immigration and the economy – have in past elections. However, Democrats do have one advantage in the midterms. They are currently seen as the preferred party (by 10 percentage points in recent polling) to fight corruption. This explains why they are spending nearly twice as much on ads about corruption than Republicans. However, should Democrats be successful and take control of Congress, they will be expected to act on this issue, and not just become part of the ongoing problem. Jared Mondschein does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
